goal_text: Write a PRD for my side project

nodes.title: What problem are you actually solving?
nodes.one_liner: Naming the pain, why it matters, and who feels it

nodes.title: Who is it for?
nodes.one_liner: Defining the user and their context of use

nodes.title: Why now, and why you?
nodes.one_liner: Motivation, insight, and what makes this worth building

nodes.title: What are you building? (Scope and features)
nodes.one_liner: Core features and what the product does

nodes.title: Drawing the line: what's explicitly out of scope
nodes.one_liner: Non-goals and cuts that keep scope honest

nodes.title: How will you know it's working?
nodes.one_liner: Success metrics and signals of progress

nodes.title: What has to be true for this to work?
nodes.one_liner: Assumptions, risks, and open questions to test

nodes.title: How does it hang together as a doc?
nodes.one_liner: Sequencing sections into a coherent PRD

outline.rationale: The user wants to learn PRD structure by writing one as a personal thinking tool, not a stakeholder artifact. I deliberately skipped process-heavy nodes (approval workflows, sign-off, formal templates, release planning, engineering handoff) since it's just for them. The outline maps to the core reasoning sections of a PRD, each framed as a question that forces a decision: problem, user, motivation, scope, non-goals, success metrics, and assumptions/risks. I separated 'scope' from 'non-goals' because articulating what you're NOT building is where PRDs earn their value and it's a distinct reasoning act. 'Why now/why you' captures the strategic framing that solo builders often skip. The final node addresses how sections cohere as a document, which serves the meta-goal of learning PRD structure. Nodes are ordered by dependency: problem→user→motivation→scope→non-goals→metrics→assumptions→assembly. Project-specific detail is deprioritized as the user confirmed they'll fill that in per section.
